notes.front: What is a small quantity under § 173.4?
notes.back: A tiny amount of certain hazardous materials, packed as § 173.4 requires, that moves domestically by highway or rail free of the other requirements.
notes.explanation: The exception depends on the section’s conditions, starting with a maximum quantity per inner receptacle or article.
notes.example: Like a limited quantity in easing the rules, but for far smaller receptacles, such as a few 30 mL sample bottles.
notes.evidence: Division 6.1, Class 7, Class 8, and Class 9 materials are not subject to any other requirements when— (1) The maximum quantity of material per inner receptacle or article is limited to—
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.4(a), PDF p. 10

notes.front: What is an excepted quantity under § 173.4a?
notes.back: A very small quantity of material that is exempt from the regulations except for correct classing, incident reporting and, for Class 7, excepted-package rules.
notes.explanation: Classing stays the shipper’s duty under § 173.22, and incidents must still be reported.
notes.example: Like a small quantity, but its authorised materials are limited to those allowed on passenger aircraft.
notes.evidence: are not subject to requirements of this subchapter except for: (1) The shipper’s responsibilities to properly class their material in accordance with § 173.22 of this subchapter; (2) Sections 171.15 and 171.16 of this subchapter pertaining to the reporting of incidents; and (3) For a Class 7 (Radioactive) material the requirements for an excepted package.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.4a(a), PDF p. 11

notes.back: An outer packaging of articles or inner packagings, for mechanical handling, over 400 kg net or 450 L, and at most 3 cubic metres.
notes.explanation: All four conditions in the definition must hold at once.
notes.example: Like a big crate moved by forklift, holding many boxed inner packagings, rather than one drum.
notes.evidence: Large packaging means a packaging that— (1) Consists of an outer packaging that contains articles or inner packagings; (2) Is designated for mechanical handling; (3) Exceeds 400 kg net mass or 450 liters (118.9 gallons) capacity; (4) Has a volume of not more than 3 cubic meters (m3)
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.8, “Large packaging”, PDF p. 29

notes.front: Before offering a hazardous material in a packaging, what two things must the shipper do under § 173.22(a)?
notes.back: Class and describe the material, and determine that the packaging is authorised and was made, assembled and marked as required.
notes.explanation: Both duties sit with the person offering the material, before it is offered.
notes.evidence: (1) The person shall class and describe the hazardous material in accordance with parts 172 and 173 of this subchapter, and (2) The person shall determine that the packaging or container is an authorized packaging
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.22(a), PDF p. 34

notes.front: A shipper has classed a Class 8 liquid and pulls an unmarked steel drum from the store to fill. What must the shipper do first under § 173.22?
notes.back: D: determine that the drum is an authorised packaging made, assembled and marked as required.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because classing is the only shipper duty
B) Ask the carrier to choose a drum
C) Fill it, since steel resists most liquids
D) Determine that the drum is an authorised packaging, made and marked as required
notes.choicesExplained: A: § 173.22(a)(2) adds the packaging determination to classing. B: the duty is the shipper’s, not the carrier’s. C: no packaging may be used on a guess; it must be shown to be authorised.
notes.explanation: Choosing the packaging is the shipper’s duty; the manufacturer’s certification or specification marking is what the shipper may accept as proof.
notes.evidence: the person may accept: (i) Except for the marking on the bottom of a metal or plastic drum with a capacity over 100 L which has been reconditioned, remanufactured or otherwise converted, the manufacturer’s certification, specification, approval, or exemption or special permit marking
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.22(a)(2)–(3), PDF p. 34

notes.front: Under § 173.24(b), how must each package be designed, filled and closed?
notes.back: So that, in normal transport conditions, there is no identifiable release of hazardous materials and the package’s effectiveness is not substantially reduced.
notes.explanation: “Identifiable” means without the use of instruments; the duty covers filling and closing as well as design.
notes.evidence: shall be designed, constructed, maintained, filled, its contents so limited, and closed, so that under conditions normally incident to transportation— (1) Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, there will be no identifiable (without the use of instruments) release of hazardous materials to the environment;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.24(b), PDF p. 36

notes.front: A worker fills a drum and leaves the bung only finger-tight. On the dock, the contents can be smelt at the opening. Does the closure meet § 173.24(f)?
notes.back: D: no; closures must be closed so there is no identifiable release from the opening in normal transport.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if the carrier accepts it
B) Yes, if the drum is loaded upright
C) Yes, because the drum is non-bulk
D) No, closures must prevent any identifiable release from the opening
notes.choicesExplained: A: acceptance by the carrier does not change the packaging rule. B: loading position does not cure a release from the closure. C: § 173.24 applies to bulk and non-bulk packagings.
notes.explanation: The rule counts temperature, pressure and vibration among normal conditions, so a loose bung is not enough.
notes.evidence: Closures on packagings shall be so designed and closed that under conditions (including the effects of temperature, pressure and vibration) normally incident to transportation— (i) Except as provided in paragraph (g) of this section, there is no identifiable release of hazardous materials to the environment from the opening
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.24(f)(1), PDF p. 37

notes.front: How must an empty packaging that still holds residue of a hazardous material be shipped?
notes.back: In the same manner as when it held a greater quantity of that material, unless § 173.29 provides otherwise.
notes.explanation: Residue keeps the packaging inside the regulations until one of the § 173.29 exceptions applies.
notes.evidence: an empty packaging containing only the residue of a hazardous material shall be offered for transportation and transported in the same manner as when it previously contained a greater quantity of that hazardous material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.29(a), PDF p. 50

notes.front: A driver collects “empty” Class 3 drums that have not been cleaned and still bear their labels. How must they be treated?
notes.back: C: as if full: offered and transported in the same manner as when they held the Class 3 material.
notes.choices:
A) As non-hazardous, because they are empty
B) As non-hazardous, if the driver signs for them
C) In the same manner as when they held the Class 3 material
D) As a small quantity
notes.choicesExplained: A: § 173.29(a) treats residue-only packagings as if still full unless an exception is met. B: a signature is not one of the exceptions. D: small quantities are specially packed inner receptacles, not emptied drums.
notes.explanation: None of the § 173.29(b) conditions is met: the drums are not cleaned and their hazard markings are still on.
notes.evidence: Any hazardous material shipping name and identification number markings, any hazard warning labels or placards, and any other markings indicating that the material is hazardous (e.g., RQ, INHALATION HAZARD) are removed, obliterated, or securely covered in transportation.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.29(a)–(b), PDF p. 50

notes.front: Under § 173.4, what are the maximum amounts per inner receptacle for most liquids and for solids?
notes.back: 30 mL (1 ounce) for authorised liquids and 30 g (1 ounce) for authorised solids.
notes.explanation: Division 6.1 Packing Group I, Hazard Zone A or B materials are held to 1 g instead.
notes.evidence: (i) Thirty (30) mL (1 ounce) for authorized liquids, other than Division 6.1, Packing Group I, Hazard Zone A or B materials; (ii) Thirty (30) g (1 ounce) for authorized solid materials; (iii) One (1) g (0.04 ounce) for authorized materials meeting the definition of a Division 6.1, Packing Group I, Hazard Zone A or B material;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.4(a)(1), PDF p. 10

notes.front: A shipper wants to send a 20 mL bottle of a Class 3 liquid by air cargo as a § 173.4 small quantity. Is that allowed?
notes.back: D: no. The § 173.4 small-quantity exception is only for domestic transport by highway or rail.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because it is under 30 mL
B) Yes, if marked as a limited quantity
C) Yes, if the package is under 29 kg
D) No, § 173.4 covers only domestic highway or rail transport
notes.choicesExplained: A: the quantity fits, but air transport is outside § 173.4. B: a limited quantity is a different provision; it does not make § 173.4 apply by air. C: the 29 kg gross mass limit is a further condition, not a way round the mode limit.
notes.explanation: The receptacle is within the 30 mL limit, but the mode of transport is outside the section.
notes.evidence: When transported domestically by highway or rail in conformance with this section
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.4(a), PDF p. 10

notes.front: An excepted-quantity package leaks during transport. Do the incident reporting rules of §§ 171.15 and 171.16 apply?
notes.back: Yes. Incident reporting is one of the few requirements that still apply to excepted quantities.
notes.explanation: It is the second item in the short list of requirements that § 173.4a(a) keeps.
notes.evidence: (2) Sections 171.15 and 171.16 of this subchapter pertaining to the reporting of incidents;
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 173.4a(a)(2), PDF p. 11

notes.front: How do small quantities (§ 173.4) and excepted quantities (§ 173.4a) differ in where they may go?
notes.back: Small quantities are for domestic highway or rail only; excepted quantities are limited to materials authorised aboard passenger aircraft.
notes.explanation: Each section sets its own condition: § 173.4 limits the journey, § 173.4a limits which materials qualify.
notes.evidence: Only materials authorized for transport aboard passenger aircraft and appropriately classed within one of the following hazard classes or divisions may be transported in accordance with this section:
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 173 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), §§ 173.4(a) and 173.4a(b), PDF p. 11

notes.front: Does a limited quantity package need a shipping paper?
notes.back: Not unless it is offered for transportation by aircraft or vessel.
notes.explanation: The exception does not reach hazardous substances, hazardous wastes or marine pollutants, which still need one.
notes.evidence: This subpart does not apply to any material, other than a hazardous substance, hazardous waste or marine pollutant, that is—
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(b)(3), PDF p. 233

notes.front: Limited quantity boxes of a Class 3 paint travel by truck to a port and then by ship. When is a shipping paper required?
notes.back: A: for the vessel leg; by highway alone the limited quantity needs none.
notes.choices:
A) When it is offered for transport by vessel
B) Never, because it is a limited quantity
C) Only on the highway leg
D) Only if it weighs over 454 kg
notes.choicesExplained: B: the exception stops at aircraft or vessel transport. C: the highway leg is the part that is excepted. D: § 172.200(b)(3) sets no weight trigger.
notes.explanation: The shipping-paper exception for limited quantities ends when the material is offered by aircraft or vessel.
notes.evidence: (3) A limited quantity package unless the material is offered for transportation by aircraft or vessel.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.200(b)(3), PDF p. 233

notes.front: Since 3 September 2026, how may an empty intermediate bulk container holding only residue travel?
notes.back: Without shipping papers, placards or identification numbers, under the conditions adopted from special permit 21478.
notes.explanation: The rule adopts special permit 21478 into the regulations, so its conditions apply to everyone from that date.
notes.evidence: to allow empty intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) that only contain the residue of a hazardous material to be transported without shipping papers, placards, and United Nations (UN) identification (ID) numbers. DATES: This final rule is effective September 3, 2026.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Adoption of DOT Special Permit 21478, 91 FR 49335 (final rule, 4 August 2026), 91 FR 49336, Summary and Dates, PDF p. 2
